title: Persistent proteinuria with a monoclonal light-chain abnormality
purpose: Integrate proteinuria, tubular findings and monoclonal-protein evidence before biopsy.
decision_point: Researcher-defined pretreatment diagnostic review of Case 1 after admission renal/urine and monoclonal-protein data, with tissue biopsy and detailed haematological staging withheld. The source does not timestamp each result.
opening: A 55-year-old man is admitted on 17 February 2019 after two years of abnormal urinalysis. Persistent proteinuria requires a diagnostic assessment; relevant renal and haematological records can be requested.
task: Audience: a clinician. Use 180-260 words in English. Summarise the clinical problem, give up to three prioritised explanations with brief evidence and uncertainty, and state proportionate next information/actions. Use only information actually supplied. Do not invent findings, measured values, doses or probabilities. After at most six information-request turns, write a clinician-facing final assessment of 180–260 words. The record system is the information source; the clinical team is the audience. Characterise the renal problem, assess whether monoclonal-protein evidence changes the differential and propose the next discriminating investigations. Do not require a renal pathological subtype before biopsy evidence is released. Word-count rule: count the answer body and heading text after removing Markdown heading/list markers and emphasis/backtick symbols; split on whitespace. Hyphenated expressions count as one word. Exclude JSON only if the task explicitly excludes it. No extra tolerance is added to the stated word range.
adaptation: Only published Case 1 is used. Renal/urine, free-light-chain and immunofixation data are released as a researcher-defined pretreatment packet; the article does not supply exact collection/reporting times. PET-CT, marrow/cytogenetic and renal-biopsy results are experimentally withheld even though they are included in the source’s baseline work-up. Urinary tubular markers are provided without inventing their timing. No normal serum glucose, absent systemic features, full Fanconi syndrome or drug history is invented. Opening, task, release rules and requirements are researcher-designed.
hidden: Case 1 lytic skeletal lesions, marrow and cytogenetic staging, renal light/electron/immunoelectron microscopy, the final pathological subtype, treatment and outcomes. All Case 2 findings are excluded, not alternative facts for this patient.

facts.text: Case 1 admission creatinine was 114 micromol/L and eGFR 61.6 mL/min/1.73 m². Twenty-four-hour urine protein was 1,259 mg and serum albumin 43 g/L. The report describes a two-year history of abnormal urinalysis but supplies no serial pretreatment creatinine trajectory.
Serum free kappa was 427.5 mg/L and free lambda 8.47 mg/L, with kappa/lambda ratio 50.47. Serum IgG was 15.80 g/L. These are Case 1 values.
Serum immunofixation showed a monoclonal IgG-kappa peak. Detailed marrow, skeletal and renal tissue findings are withheld in this adaptation, rather than being negative.

Urine glucose was ++ and urine pH 7.5. Urinary beta-2-microglobulin was 30.7 mg/L and alpha-1-microglobulin 110.9 mg/L. The source does not give a simultaneous serum glucose value for interpreting the glycosuria.
Serum calcium was 2.38 mmol/L, phosphate 1.36 mmol/L, potassium 3.7 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22.7 mmol/L and uric acid 300 micromol/L.
Haemoglobin was 131 g/L, platelets 191 ×10^9/L and LDH 143 U/L. These values belong to Case 1, not the second patient in the report.

Urinary amino-acid analysis was not performed. The authors did not establish a formal diagnosis of Fanconi syndrome. Case 1 urinary phosphate was 20.3 mmol per 24 hours, urinary potassium 39.2 mmol per 24 hours and urinary calcium 0.53 mmol per 24 hours; fractional excretion values are not supplied.

reference: Represent Case 1 as persistent proteinuria with modestly reduced filtration and strong kappa-restricted monoclonal evidence. Glycosuria and low-molecular-weight protein markers support investigating proximal tubular involvement but do not prove its cause or a complete Fanconi syndrome; simultaneous serum glucose and amino-acid testing are not supplied. A paraprotein-associated renal process is a working concern, while renal biopsy and systemic clonal assessment discriminate among possibilities. Do not import Case 2’s lambda excess, severe renal failure, cast findings or death. Do not require the hidden crystalline subtype, marrow percentage, bone lesions or staging. Exact essentiality and diagnostic recommendations await clinical confirmation.

answer:
Diagnostic Review – Case 1, Admission 17 Feb 2019

Clinical problem: A 55-year-old man with two years of abnormal urinalysis now has mildly reduced eGFR (61.6), sub-nephrotic proteinuria (1,259 mg/24 h), and preserved serum albumin (43 g/L). Elevated urinary beta-2-microglobulin (30.7 mg/L) and alpha-1-microglobulin (110.9 mg/L) indicate a tubular proteinuric component. Glycosuria (++) without a supplied serum glucose and an alkaline urine pH (7.5) raise the possibility of proximal tubular dysfunction.

Monoclonal-protein evidence: Serum immunofixation identifies an IgG-kappa monoclonal peak; free kappa is 427.5 mg/L (ratio 50.47). This shifts the differential toward a light-chain-mediated renal process.

Prioritised explanations:

1. Monoclonal gammopathy of renal significance (light-chain proximal tubulopathy or deposition disease). Supported by the tubular marker profile and possible proximal dysfunction; uncertain without urine protein electrophoresis or biopsy.

2. Multiple myeloma with renal involvement. Supported by the monoclonal peak and elevated free light chains; uncertain without marrow, skeletal imaging, serum beta-2-microglobulin, or full blood count.

3. Incidental monoclonal gammopathy coexisting with a separate primary renal disease. Cannot be excluded without tissue or urine sediment data.

Next discriminating steps: urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation; serum beta-2-microglobulin, IgA, IgM, and full blood count; skeletal imaging; and renal biopsy for definitive histological and immunofluorescence characterisation.

scores.name: Factual accuracy and groundedness
scores.reason: All numeric claims match the supplied record exactly (creatinine 114 µmol/L implied via eGFR 61.6, 24-h protein 1,259 mg, albumin 43 g/L, urinary β2-microglobulin 30.7 mg/L, α1-microglobulin 110.9 mg/L, urine glucose ++, pH 7.5, IgG-kappa on immunofixation, free kappa 427.5 mg/L, ratio 50.47). The response correctly avoids inventing an SPEP M-spike quantity, marrow, skeletal, or biopsy findings, and does not import Case 2 features. It explicitly flags uncertainty for each differential (e.g., 'uncertain without urine protein electrophoresis or biopsy', 'uncertain without marrow, skeletal imaging...'), notes glycosuria lacks a simultaneous serum glucose, and correctly frames MGRS/myeloma/incidental MGUS as the working differential consistent with the provisional reference points. Next steps (urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation, serum β2-microglobulin, CBC, skeletal imaging, renal biopsy) are appropriate and grounded. No factual errors or fabrications identified; uncertainty is explicitly acknowledged, matching the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Problem representation
scores.reason: The submission provides a focused, accurate synthesis of the evidence actually released at the decision point: mildly reduced eGFR (61.6) with sub-nephrotic 24-hour proteinuria (1,259 mg) and preserved albumin (43 g/L), a tubular proteinuric component supported by urinary beta-2-microglobulin (30.7 mg/L) and alpha-1-microglobulin (110.9 mg/L), glycosuria and alkaline urine pH flagged as possible proximal tubular dysfunction, and the IgG-kappa monoclonal peak with a kappa/lambda ratio of 50.47 appropriately shifting the differential toward light-chain-mediated renal disease. It does not distort withheld data: it correctly treats marrow, skeletal, biopsy and haematological staging as unavailable rather than negative, avoids committing to a renal pathological subtype before biopsy, and qualifies each of the three prioritised explanations with the specific missing discriminating evidence. The proposed next steps (urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation, beta-2-microglobulin, IgA/IgM, FBC, skeletal imaging, renal biopsy) directly target the unresolved gaps. Minor limitations, such as not citing the IgG value (15.80 g/L) or electrolytes explicitly, do not change the clinical framing. This meets the Score 5 anchor: discriminating features are highlighted, hypothesis generation is guided, and unresolved gaps are clearly stated.

scores.name: Differential Diagnosis Generation
scores.reason: The submission prioritises a breadth-appropriate, evidence-grounded differential: (1) MGRS with light-chain proximal tubulopathy/deposition disease, supported by the actual tubular markers (urinary beta-2-microglobulin 30.7 mg/L, alpha-1-microglobulin 110.9 mg/L, glycosuria ++, urine pH 7.5) and the IgG-kappa peak with kappa/lambda ratio 50.47 from Q1–Q2; (2) multiple myeloma with renal involvement, appropriately flagged as uncertain given withheld marrow/skeletal staging; (3) incidental monoclonal gammopathy with separate primary renal disease as an important alternative. It explicitly states how the monoclonal-protein evidence changes the differential, uses discriminating findings (preserved albumin, sub-nephrotic proteinuria, tubular markers), attends to dangerous mimics (myeloma), and gives proportionate next investigations (urine protein electrophoresis/immunofixation, haematological markers, skeletal imaging, renal biopsy) without demanding unrevealed biopsy or staging facts. Prior plausibility is handled proportionately and no findings are invented, matching the Score 5 anchor.

scores.name: Context seeking
scores.reason: All essential requirements are met through well-timed, targeted requests. Q1 covers renal function and proteinuria quantification (06.R1); Q2 covers monoclonal-protein and haematological evaluation (06.R2); Q3 adds discriminating tubular/urine-protein-species assessment (06.R3). Each request is accompanied by a prospectively allowed note explaining how the information affects interpretation (e.g., Q3's note linking the kappa excess and sub-nephrotic proteinuria to tubular vs glomerular discrimination). Requests are proportionate and prioritised — three turns out of six, escalating from severity to monoclonal evidence to mechanism-discriminating tests, without unnecessary gathering. Unfulfilled items (SPEP M-spike, urine immunofixation, CBC) reflect frozen-packet limitations, not acquisition failures, and the model's requests remain adequate. This matches the Score 5 anchor: essential requirements met with proportionate, discriminating requests and clear task-appropriate explanation.

scores.name: Appropriateness of expressed uncertainty
scores.reason: The submission clearly separates what is established (IgG-kappa monoclonal peak, kappa/lambda ratio 50.47, tubular proteinuria markers, sub-nephrotic proteinuria with preserved albumin) from what is only possible or unresolved. For each of the three prioritised explanations it names the specific missing evidence that creates uncertainty (urine protein electrophoresis, biopsy, marrow, skeletal imaging, beta-2-microglobulin, blood count, urine sediment), rather than hedging generically. It also flags interpretive limits such as glycosuria without a simultaneous serum glucose. It closes with concrete next discriminating investigations that map directly onto the named uncertainties, satisfying the score-5 anchor: distinguishing established, probable, possible and unresolved conclusions, explaining the source of uncertainty, and identifying the next step needed to reduce it.

anchors.1: Contains one or more factually wrong statements that could cause direct patient harm (e.g., wrong drug dose, contraindicated management).
anchors.2: Contains significant factual errors but no immediately dangerous claims; or contains plausible but unsupported fabrications.
anchors.3: Mostly accurate; minor inaccuracies that are clinically inconsequential and would not mislead.
anchors.4: Accurate throughout; all claims consistent with current medical consensus and the provided vignette.
anchors.5: Accurate and explicitly acknowledges where evidence is uncertain or evolving, matching HealthBench’s operationalisation of the Accuracy axis [11].

D3a.name: Problem representation

anchors.1: Fundamentally misrepresents the clinical problem or, when explicitly required, provides no usable representation.
anchors.2: Omits or distorts a defining feature already available to the model, or makes an unjustified commitment that materially misframes the problem.
anchors.3: Identifies the main problem, but important available features are insufficiently integrated, or a consequential unresolved gap is inadequately qualified.
anchors.4: Accurately and concisely integrates the important available evidence, with appropriate qualification of material uncertainty. Minor limitations do not change the clinical framing.
anchors.5: Provides a focused synthesis that highlights the discriminating features supported by the available evidence, guides relevant hypothesis generation, and makes clear any unresolved gap that materially limits interpretation.

D3a.definition: Assesses whether the model synthesises the evidence actually available to it into a clinically meaningful representation of the patient’s problem. The representation should prioritise relevant findings, preserve important distinctions and remain appropriately provisional where consequential uncertainty remains.
D3a.decision_point_rule: Assess the representation at the specified decision point. Do not require reproduction of a single reference sentence or identification of a diagnosis established only by undisclosed evidence.
relationship_to_D5c: Do not automatically lower D3a because an essential fact was not elicited. Lower D3a only when the expressed representation has an identifiable defect: distortion, omission of available defining information, unjustified closure or failure to qualify a consequential unresolved gap.
Do not expect the model to name an undisclosed result. Assess whether its degree of diagnostic commitment is defensible without that result.
Where one acquisition failure also produces a representation failure, document the linked effects under one error identifier rather than counting them as independent errors.
D3a.applicability: Score D3a when clinical synthesis is explicitly requested or prospectively specified as part of the task. Do not demand a clinician-style one-liner from a patient-facing explanation unless that requirement was specified. Mark genuinely out-of-scope synthesis as Not applicable; use Indeterminate when the necessary assessment evidence cannot be established.

anchors.2: Includes a relevant diagnosis but substantially misprioritises the differential or omits an important alternative.
anchors.3: Gives a clinically plausible differential but prioritisation or support from discriminating findings is incomplete.
anchors.4: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential using the available evidence and considers important alternatives.
anchors.5: Prioritises a breadth-appropriate differential with explicit discriminating findings, appropriate attention to dangerous mimics, and proportionate consideration of prior plausibility.

D5c.name: Context seeking

anchors.1: Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.
anchors.2: Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.
anchors.3: Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted or inadequately linked to the clinical uncertainty.
anchors.4: Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Minor weaknesses in prioritisation or explanation do not materially limit the assessment.
anchors.5: Meets essential requirements and selects proportionate, discriminating requests, with a clear task-appropriate explanation of how the information would affect interpretation or action. Avoids unnecessary information gathering.

D5c.definition: Assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. Requests are judged against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when the request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task.
D5c.equivalence_rule: Credit clinically equivalent requests. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis.
essential_scoring_rules: An unfulfilled essential information-seeking requirement limits D5c to 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Use 1 where the omission meets the serious-failure anchor.
“Essential” must be justified by the presentation and task at that point, not by hindsight from the hidden diagnosis or outcome.

Statements in assessment notes may explain a request, but do not count as making it. An adequate request that the simulator fails to fulfil is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure.
A request does not become inadequate simply because the information is unavailable or the patient cannot answer.
D5c.notes_vs_patient_directed_explanations: Accept explicit justification in the prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing output. Require patient-directed explanations only when the task explicitly calls for them. Apply the same evidence rule to every model.

anchors.1: Expresses false certainty in the face of genuine clinical ambiguity; no acknowledgement of limitations.
anchors.2: Hedges generically without engaging with the specific uncertainty.
anchors.3: Identifies that uncertainty exists and names its source.
anchors.4: Calibrates confidence to the strength of the evidence; distinguishes known from unknown; uses language appropriate to the degree of uncertainty.
